sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Indiana, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Thursday, October 22Passed

Your application must be in the hands of election officials by 11:59 p.m. on Thursday, October 22, 2026 (the law says 12 days before the election). A postmark does not count: an application that arrives later is not processed, even if mailed earlier. You need a new application for each election. (official page)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your county election officials must have your ballot by 6 p.m. (local time) on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. A postmark does not count, even one dated on or before Election Day. (official page)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Monday, November 2, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Indiana’s own site

At school away from home, in Indiana or in another state? What Indiana says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

Yes. To vote by mail you must be able to mark your own ballot and sign the envelope, and have one of the reasons in state law: you expect to be away from your county for all 12 hours the polls are open (6 a.m. to 6 p.m.); you have a disability; you are 65 or older; you have election duties outside your precinct; you are scheduled to work at your regular job for all 12 hours; you are confined by illness or injury, or caring for someone who is, for all 12 hours; a religious practice or holiday keeps you from voting all 12 hours; you are in the state's address confidentiality program; you are in the military or a public safety officer; you are a 'serious sex offender' as state law defines it; or you have no transportation to the polls. (official page)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Log in to your voter portal at IndianaVoters.in.gov, choose 'ABS-Mail' and fill it in. You do not need to sign it; the system uses the signature on your voter record. Open it (official page)
  • Mail or in person. Fill out the ABS-Mail application and mail it or hand it in to your county election board. You can print it, call your county or the Indiana Election Division at (317) 232-3939 to have one mailed, or pick one up at the county office. Open it (official page)
  • By e-mail. Print, sign, and scan or photograph the application (and your ID copy, if you use one) and e-mail it to your county election official or to the Indiana Election Division. (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it in the postage-paid return envelope that comes with the ballot, early enough to arrive by 6 p.m. on Election Day. (official page)
  • In person. Hand-deliver it to your county election board, including an early voting location, by 6 p.m. on Election Day. Only you, a member of your household or family, your attorney-in-fact (power of attorney), or a bonded courier may deliver it; anyone but you fills out an ABS-19 affidavit. (official page)

What the envelope needs

Your application must include either a photocopy of an ID that meets the state's photo ID law, or one of these numbers: your Indiana driver's license or state ID number, your voter ID number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number (giving more than one is recommended). Sign the ballot security envelope; no witness is needed. You may not have help marking a mail ballot, but you may have help sealing the envelope (the helper fills out an affidavit and cannot be your employer or union representative). Some first-time voters who registered by paper must also send proof of where they live (such as a utility bill or bank statement) with the ABS-12 form; without it the ballot is treated as provisional until the proof reaches the county by 6 p.m. on Election Day. If you forget to sign or make a mistake, you can fix it before Election Day with form ABS-5. (official page)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Indiana’s own site (federal guide)

Vote early in person instead

Tuesday, October 6, 2026 to Monday, November 2, 2026.

In-person absentee voting (early voting) is open for 28 days before the election and ends at noon (local time) on the day before the election; every county must also be open the two Saturdays just before Election Day. Each county sets its own dates, hours and places, listed at IndianaVoters.in.gov. Bring a photo ID that meets the state's law. (official page)

Students

At school in Indiana, away from home

Indiana says college students may register at only one of two places: the address where they live while attending school, or the address where they live when not attending school. Where they plan to return after college or during breaks is not part of the decision; they may register at school if they choose. State law forbids challenging a voter only because they are a student or live in student housing. A student registered at home in another county who will be away from that county all of Election Day can ask that county for a mail ballot (being away from the county all 12 hours is one of the reasons allowed). (official page)

At school in another state, with Indiana as home

The state's pages do not speak to Indiana students at school in other states separately. Its general rules: you may stay registered at your Indiana home address, and if you expect to be away from your county for all 12 hours the polls are open you may ask for a mail ballot, which must be back in your county's hands by 6 p.m. on Election Day (a postmark does not count). A student from another state going to school in Indiana may register at the Indiana address where they live while attending school. (official page)

Military and overseas

Military members, their families and overseas voters use the Federal Post Card Application, with a copy of a photo ID or one of the ID numbers listed above. A request for a mailed ballot must be received by 11:59 p.m. on October 22, 2026; a request for a ballot sent by e-mail, online or fax by noon on Monday, November 2, 2026. Ballots returned from inside the U.S., and ballots e-mailed or faxed, must be received by 6 p.m. on November 3. A ballot mailed from outside the U.S. must be postmarked by November 3 and received by noon on the tenth day after the election (Friday, November 13, 2026). Military and overseas voters can register by mail (received by October 26, 2026) or by e-mail or fax (received by 11:59 p.m. on October 26, 2026). (federal guide)

Indiana in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • The deadline to ask for a mail ballot is 11:59 p.m. on Thursday, October 22, 2026, one day after this check. After that, voting early in person (until noon on Monday, November 2) or on Election Day are the remaining ways to vote, except for military and overseas voters.
  • If you asked for a mail ballot and it never came, you can sign an affidavit (form PRE-5) at your polling place on Election Day and vote a regular ballot, if otherwise qualified.
  • In Indiana, early voting in person is called 'in-person absentee voting'. The early voting dates here come from the state's rule (28 days before, through noon the day before); your county's exact days and hours are on IndianaVoters.in.gov.
Where this comes from: 4 pages of Indiana’s election office, its laws and the federal guide
  1. Absentee Voting, Indiana Secretary of State, Election Division (official page; read October 21, 2026)
  2. College Students, Indiana Secretary of State, Election Division (official page; read October 21, 2026)
  3. Indiana 2026-2027 Voting Assistance Guide, Federal Voting Assistance Program (U.S. Department of Defense) (federal guide; read October 21, 2026)
  4. Indiana Voters portal (ballot status), as named in the Indiana 2026-2027 Voting Assistance Guide, Federal Voting Assistance Program (U.S. Department of Defense) (federal guide; read October 21, 2026)

Checked October 21, 2026. Rules and dates can change: Indiana’s election office, and your county or local election office, have the final word.

polls:
Polls are open 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time. (source)

  • rest of the state: 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. EST
  • Twelve counties in the northwest and the southwest corners: 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. CST

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
